one_liner: Safe, no_std-capable Rust port of Google's Brotli encoder and decoder; slower than the C reference, not faster.
what_it_does: The brotli crate is a line-by-line port of google/brotli's compressor (and, through its brotli-decompressor dependency, the decompressor) to Rust, with io::Read/io::Write wrappers (CompressorReader, CompressorWriter, Decompressor, DecompressorWriter), one-shot BrotliCompress/BrotliDecompress stream copies, and a manual BrotliState/BrotliDecompressStream interface that mirrors the C API. It runs without the Rust standard library behind a pluggable allocator, and an optional ffi-api feature builds a libbrotli.so (cd c && make) that the README calls a drop-in replacement for the C library. Extras over C include multithreaded single-file compression (compress_multi), catable/appendable streams with a catbrotli tool, custom and serialized shared dictionaries (9.0.0), and a validation mode.
how_it_is_fast: It is not faster than the baseline: it reuses the same algorithms as C Brotli (LZ77 with hash-chain or binary-tree matchers, context modeling, Huffman coding) in safe Rust, so speed tracks C minus safety costs. The decompressor README names the expected losses: an extra indirection in the Huffman-group tables, array bounds checks on every access, and no aligned 64- or 128-bit loads from a byte slice. brotli-decompressor's optional unsafe feature swaps slice indexing for get_unchecked and skips memory initialisation, and its 6.1.0/6.1.1 releases (October 2026) add bulk back-reference and dictionary copies, a faster bit-reader refill and leaner Huffman-tree lookups, none of which has published numbers.
when_to_use: You need the Brotli format in pure safe Rust: wasm, cross-compiles without a C toolchain, or a no_std kernel or embedded target with your own allocator.
Sandboxed decoding where every allocation is front-loaded into a memory pool before SECCOMP or a similar jail is switched on.
Splitting work across cores or chunks: compress_multi for multithreaded compression of one buffer, or catable/appendable streams joined by byte concatenation or catbrotli.
HTTP content-encoding in Rust servers at moderate quality (tower-http depends on it and sets quality 4), where encoder CPU rather than decode throughput is the concern.
Brotli with custom LZ77 prefix dictionaries or serialized shared dictionaries (draft-vandevenne-shared-brotli-format) from Rust.
when_not_to_use: Decode throughput matters: every published number puts it behind C, from 72-82% of C speed (Dropbox 2016) to 1.56x slower in a 2026 third-party test; that project (android-doctor) switched to vendored C libbrotli 1.1.0 and cut its firmware extraction from 4.65 s to 2.28 s.

You can choose the format: the catalog's zstd and LZ4 entries report decompression at 1,550 and 4,970 MB/s, far above the 250-391 MB/s Brotli decode figures here (different hardware, so only indicative).

You want the newest decoder optimisations through this crate: brotli 9.0.0 pins brotli-decompressor ~6.0 (>=6.0.0, <6.1.0), so the 6.1.x speed work is only reachable by depending on brotli-decompressor directly for decoding.

Your policy excludes AI-authored code: brotli-decompressor 6.0.0's changelog says its commits were 'effectively authored by Claude' and advises such users to stay on 5.x, which brotli 9.0.0 cannot use.
You need bit-exact output with C at quality 10 or 11: the README only promises identical output at levels 0-9.

integration.form: crate (brotli on crates.io); optional C shared library via the ffi-api feature
integration.dependencies: alloc-no-stdlib 3.x, brotli-decompressor ~6.0, alloc-stdlib 0.3.x with the default std feature; sha2 ~0.10 only with the validation feature
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.59 (rust-version), edition 2015; the simd feature needs nightly
integration.platforms: any Rust target; no_std with default-features = false; no hardware SIMD unless the nightly simd feature is enabled
integration.thread_safety: Not documented for the stream objects; each Compressor/Decompressor owns its state, and compress_multi requires Send allocators per thread. 9.0.0 fixed #257, where the FFI's SendableMemoryBlock<T> claimed Send for non-Send T.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — the ffi-api build exports the C libbrotli interface (README: drop-in for google/brotli), but the FFI has been off by default since 5.0.0 to avoid symbol conflicts, and the Rust API is not the C API.

gotchas: BrotliEncoderParams::default() uses quality 11 (lgwin 22), which is very slow; issue #93 (open since 2023-03-21) asks for a lower default, and tower-http overrides it to 4.

Quality 10 is reused as a proxy for '9.5' (a hash-chain H9 mode) in the one-shot compressor, so it does not mean C's quality 10; the portable-float feature also changes emitted bytes (about 0.006% ratio).

brotli 9.0.0 has no unsafe feature of its own; brotli-decompressor's unsafe feature (get_unchecked indexing, no memory initialisation) is only reachable by adding that crate directly with the feature enabled so Cargo unifies it.

The Cargo description says all included code is safe and the README excepts only the FFI bindings, but the seccomp feature turns on alloc-no-stdlib's unsafe calloc-backed pools; the 'safe' feature removes the FFI's unsafe Send impls along with the encoder and multicompress FFI entry points.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Choose it over the C codecs in this category (zstd, LZ4, zlib-ng, libdeflate) only when the Brotli format is required and a pure safe-Rust, no_std or C-toolchain-free build matters more than speed. Unlike lz4_flex, which matches or beats its C reference, this port trails C Brotli decoding by roughly 1.2x to 2x.
verified_claims_summary: Dropbox's 2016 post, seen only as search snippets because dropbox.tech does not resolve here, measured the safe Rust decompressor at 217 MB/s, 72% of the C decompressor built with gcc-4.9 -O3, on 4 MB blocks on an Intel Core i7-4790 at 3.60 GHz, rising to 249 MB/s (82%) with the unsafe feature; the Rust toolchain was not stated and no benchmark code is public. Independently, android-doctor issue #74 (October 2026, 10-core Apple Silicon, release build) measured brotli 9.0 decoding at 250 MB/s against 391 MB/s for C via Python brotli (1.56x slower), then 4.65 s against 2.28 s end to end after switching to vendored libbrotli 1.1.0; neither run states quality, Python brotli version or compiler flags, and both predate brotli-decompressor 6.1.x. No compression-speed comparison with C exists.
status_note: Actively maintained (9.0.0 on 2026-09-02, brotli-decompressor 6.1.1 on 2026-10-21), BSD-3-Clause AND MIT, about 302.6 million crates.io downloads; the safe, portable Brotli choice in Rust, not the fast one.
